rv.q: By the end of the show, you'll swear that truck can dance.
Although it’s far from fully loaded in a conventional sense, this scrappy, sincere new musical brings a fresh, handmade feeling to Broadway, which mostly traffics in the machine tooled.
That makes this gently appealing show a welcome change of pace, even if its folksy simplicity makes it a commercial challenge.
For all the worthy effort to valorize lives not usually depicted in musicals, this has the opposite effect: It makes them seem petty.
The musical adaptation of S.R. Bindler's documentary about a Texas endurance contest has heart, soul and honky-tonk authenticity, but it needs more theatrical juice to make it on Broadway.
While not as dull as watching paint dry on a four-wheeler, Hardbody has too puny an engine to take anyone very far.

But if you go into the show wondering why a gifted creative team would want to adapt the 1997 documentary about poor Texans in an endurance contest for a red Nissan pickup, you are likely to leave wondering the same thing.
Rarely has so much goodwill been so squandered.
The resulting confusion of tone proves fatal.
With all that going for it, Hardbody holds up better than you might expect.
Neil Pepe's production is quite gripping - most impressive is how the actors manipulate the vehicle and perform dance choreography while their hands are still attached to it.

If you only see only one musical this year loosely based on a 1997 documentary about people in Texas trying to win a Nissan truck by being the last person to keep their hand on it, it may as well be Hands on a Hardbody.
There's nothing unlikable about 'Hands on a Hardbody,' but little to love, either.
As is, it’s a bit of a missed opportunity.

The tuner coarsens its self-effacing, quietly observant source with cheesy soap-opera backstories, forced Lifetime-movie subplotting, and self-righteous hot-button-issue pressing in an obviously manipulative attempt to stir our emotions.
The show's biggest problem is that it doesn't know what it wants to be.
Unfortunately, the music – a mix of country, rock and bluegrass – falls short of inspiring.
